meta.title: Who really said "Failure is only the opportunity more intelligently to begin again"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Henry Ford's 1922 book really carries it — verbatim, in the introduction to My Life and Work (with Samuel Crowther). Most versions online have the words quietly reordered.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Failure is only the opportunity more intelligently to begin again'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: this exact sentence is in Henry Ford's My Life and Work (1922). The popular 'simply… this time more intelligently' version is a rewrite.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1863–1947 · American industrialist, founder of the Ford Motor Company
answer.sourceLine: Confirmed verbatim, word for word, in the introduction to My Life and Work (1922), the memoir Ford produced in collaboration with the journalist Samuel Crowther. The sentence sits between “One who fears the future, who fears failure, limits his activities” and “There is no disgrace in honest failure; there is disgrace in fearing to fail” — you can read it in place in the full text at Project Gutenberg ↗.

source.heading: Where it comes from

docMeta.dd: Henry Ford, in collaboration with Samuel Crowther

source.excerpt: 1. An absence of fear of the future and of veneration for the past. One who fears the future, who fears failure, limits his activities. Failure is only the opportunity more intelligently to begin again. There is no disgrace in honest failure; there is disgrace in fearing to fail. What is past is useful only as it suggests ways and means for progress.
trail: Project Gutenberg’s full text ↗ of My Life and Work carries the sentence word for word in the introduction, “What Is the Idea?” — the wording shown above is the printed wording, character for character; the version most often circulated online is not.

Quote Investigator ↗ reaches the same place, concluding: “Henry Ford did write a book with a co-author in 1922 that contained the quotation although the phrasing differed slightly from the modern common version.”
Quote Investigator also logs the introduction’s reprinting in McClure’s for May 1922 and a reordered wording in Engineering Production for 21 December 1922, on the same page ↗.
Wikiquote ↗ lists the line in its sourced section for My Life and Work at pp. 19–20, and the Internet Archive scan ↗ confirms the 1922 Doubleday, Page printing.
source.excerptNote: The passage is the first of four principles Ford sets out at the close of the introduction, reproduced here with the numeral and opening sentence exactly as they stand on the page.

author.name: Henry Ford
author.heading: Who was Henry Ford?
author.metaLine: 1863–1947 · American industrialist, founder of the Ford Motor Company
author.bio: Ford founded the Ford Motor Company in 1903, launched the Model T in 1908, and moved his plants onto a moving assembly line in 1913 — changes that made the car an ordinary object and remade industrial work along with it. He was not himself a writer: My Life and Work and its sequels were published “in collaboration with” the journalist Samuel Crowther, who shaped Ford’s thinking into prose. His legacy is not uncomplicated — from 1920 his newspaper The Dearborn Independent ran a long run of antisemitic articles, later collected as The International Jew.

misattribution.heading: The wording problem
misattribution.intro: Nobody is stealing this line from Henry Ford — it really is his book’s sentence. What goes wrong is the wording: almost every version in circulation has been reordered or smoothed, and the tidiest one is the furthest from the page.

items.who: “Failure is simply the opportunity to begin again, this time more intelligently.”
items.why: The most widely circulated version, and not what the book says. BrainyQuote ↗ serves it under Ford’s name with no source citation at all.

items.who: “Failure is only the opportunity to begin again more intelligently.”
items.why: The adverb moved almost immediately. Quote Investigator ↗ records this reordered form in Engineering Production of 21 December 1922 — within months of the book’s publication.

items.who: “Failure is only the opportunity to more intelligently begin again.”
items.why: Wikiquote ↗ correctly files the line as sourced to My Life and Work at pp. 19–20, but transcribes it with the adverb shifted — a reminder to check the book, not the quote page.

The book’s own title is “My Life and Work by Henry Ford in Collaboration with Samuel Crowther” — that is how the Garden City reprint ↗ is catalogued. Crowther, a journalist, shaped the memoir for publication, so the sentence carries a collaborator’s polish as well as Ford’s idea.

misattribution.truthLine: The genuine 1922 sentence — the one actually printed in the book — is “Failure is only the opportunity more intelligently to begin again.” Read it in place in the Project Gutenberg text ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Ford opened My Life and Work not with a car but with a creed. The introduction closes on four principles behind the company, and the first is “An absence of fear of the future and of veneration for the past.” The failure sentence is the gloss on that principle — a working rule for a factory, not a motivational poster.

The book landed in 1922, when Ford was one of the most famous industrialists in the world, and the words travelled fast: the introduction was reprinted in McClure’s that May, and by December a trade paper was already quoting the line — with the adverb moved. That early reach is exactly why the wording drifted, and why the smoothed modern version eventually overtook the original.
context.detailsSummary: The rest of Ford’s four principles
detailsBody: The introduction lists four: an absence of fear of the future and of veneration for the past; a disregard of competition; the putting of service before profit; and that manufacturing is not buying low and selling high. The failure line belongs to the first of them.
The same paragraph closes on a sentence that is arguably sharper than the famous one: “What is past is useful only as it suggests ways and means for progress.”
context.pull: “There is no disgrace in honest failure; there is disgrace in fearing to fail.”
